title: Evaluation pipelines: offline, online, golden sets, regressions
story:
A change to a system that produces language cannot be judged by running it once. The output differs between runs, the thing you are measuring is a distribution rather than a value, and the person judging is the person who made the change. Every part of that is a problem.

The fix has two halves that measure different things. Offline evaluation runs a fixed set of cases with known-good answers and scores every change automatically, which gives you repeatability and speed — you can run it on every commit. Online evaluation exposes the change to real traffic against a control and measures what actually happened, which gives you validity. Neither substitutes for the other: offline tells you quickly whether something broke, online tells you slowly whether anything improved.

The fixed set is where the discipline lives, and the failure is subtle enough to be worth stating carefully. Every time you compare a change against that set and keep the winner, you have selected on it. Dwork and colleagues put the general form precisely: existing approaches to ensuring validity of inferences assume a fixed procedure selected before the data are examined, whereas in practice data analysis is intrinsically adaptive, with new analyses generated based on data exploration and on the results of previous analyses on the same data. After enough iterations, your evaluation set no longer estimates quality — it describes what you tuned toward.

That is not hypothetical, and the scale is worth knowing. A survey of fields that adopted these methods found leakage in 17 of them, affecting 294 papers, in some cases producing wildly overoptimistic conclusions, with a taxonomy of eight types ranging from textbook errors to open research problems. Published, reviewed work, measured wrongly.

So the practices that follow. Keep a held-out portion of the evaluation set that is consulted rarely and deliberately, because the working set is spent. Refresh cases over time, since a static set ages toward the cases you have already fixed. Treat every regression as a new case rather than a fix — the bug you shipped is the best evaluation case you will ever get, and it is free. And be explicit that the offline number is a regression detector rather than a quality measure: it is excellent at telling you something got worse and poor at telling you something got better, which is precisely why the online half exists.

problem.name: Evaluation against a fixed set
problem.shape: A change must be judged on a system whose output varies between runs, by the person who made the change.
tell: quality is assessed by trying a few examples by hand
the evaluation set has been used for every decision for months
an offline improvement did not survive contact with users
a shipped bug was fixed without being added to the set
problem.move: Run a fixed set automatically on every change to catch regressions, and confirm anything that looks like an improvement on live traffic against a control. Hold back a portion of the set that is consulted rarely, refresh cases as the system improves, and add every shipped bug as a case.
problem.invariant: A set used to choose between changes is being selected on, so its score stops being an estimate of quality and becomes a description of what was tuned toward.
problem.breaks: Offline and online measure different things, and offline can improve while online does not — the set is a sample of cases somebody chose, and it will not contain the traffic pattern that actually matters unless somebody thought of it. So a clean offline result is evidence against regression rather than evidence of improvement.

cost.time: building and maintaining the cases, which is continuous work nobody is assigned
cost.space: the cases and their expected outputs, versioned alongside the system
cost.beats: trying examples by hand, which is unrepeatable and biased toward the cases you already have in mind, and shipping to measure, which is valid and slow and occasionally expensive

worked.problem: Why might an improvement on your evaluation set not be an improvement?
worked.reasoning:
Three reasons, and they are separate failures with separate fixes.

The first is selection. Every time you compare candidates against the set and keep the best, you are choosing on it — and the best of several noisy measurements is biased upward by roughly the noise, which is the point the three-way-split lesson made. Do that for months and the set no longer estimates quality; it describes what you tuned toward. The general statement is that approaches to ensuring validity assume a fixed procedure selected before the data are examined, while real analysis is intrinsically adaptive, generating new analyses from exploration and from previous results on the same data. Every decision made after seeing the score is one of those adaptive steps.

The second is coverage. The set is a sample of cases somebody chose, and it contains the situations that person thought of. Real traffic contains the situations they did not. So a change can improve every case in the set and degrade a pattern that is common in production and absent from the set — and nothing in the offline number can reveal that, because the evidence is not in the file.

The third is that the metric may not track what you care about. An automatic score is a proxy, and proxies are optimisable independently of the thing they proxy for. A change that improves the score by making answers longer, or more hedged, or more similar to the reference phrasing, has improved the measurement rather than the system.

That last one is why the online half exists. Exposing the change to real traffic against a control measures what actually happened rather than what a proxy predicted, and the control is what separates the effect of the change from everything else moving that week.

The scale of the general problem is worth citing rather than asserting. A survey of fields adopting these methods found leakage in 17 of them, affecting 294 papers, in some cases producing wildly overoptimistic conclusions, with a taxonomy of eight types from textbook errors to open research problems. That is published work, reviewed, and measured wrongly — so the assumption that careful people do not make this error is not supported.

Practically: hold back a portion of the set consulted rarely and deliberately, refresh cases as the system improves past the old ones, add every shipped bug as a case since it is the best evaluation case you will ever get and it is free, and be explicit about what the offline number is. It is a regression detector — excellent at telling you something got worse, poor at telling you something got better.

problem.practice: Count how many decisions your evaluation set has been used to make. Then take the last three changes that improved it and check whether any was confirmed on live traffic. Finally, look at your last shipped bug and check whether it is now a case.

beats.broke: A change to a system that produces language cannot be judged by running it once, because the output differs every time and the thing being measured is a distribution rather than a value.
beats.fix: Build a fixed set of cases with known-good answers and score every change against it automatically, then confirm offline improvements on live traffic, because the two measure different things.
beats.cost: The fixed set is selected against on every change, so it stops being an unbiased estimate and becomes a description of what you tuned toward — and it must be refreshed by somebody deciding what belongs in it.

interview.q: Why might an improvement on your evaluation set not be an improvement?
interview.trap: Naming only overfitting to the set. Coverage and proxy-optimisation are separate failures — the set contains what somebody thought of, and an automatic metric can be improved by making answers longer or more hedged without improving anything.
interview.answer:
Three reasons, and they are separate failures with separate fixes.

And the metric is a proxy, which is optimisable independently of what it proxies for. A change that improves the score by making answers longer, more hedged, or closer to the reference phrasing has improved the measurement rather than the system. That is why the online half exists — real traffic against a control measures what happened rather than what a proxy predicted, and the control separates the change from everything else moving that week.
